title: Beatles attraction at 3 Savile Row approved – with ban on rooftop gigs
summary:
Westminster council signs off on ‘cultural experience and exhibition’ at site where band last performed in public

Fans of the Beatles will be able to stand on the Savile Row rooftop where…

blocks.text: Fans of the Beatles will be able to stand on the Savile Row rooftop in London where the band held their final public performance, but any visitors hoping to experience what made the site a famed rock destination will be disappointed – because live music will be banned.

Westminster city council has voted on proposals to turn the Grade-II listed building at 3 Savile Row in central London into a seven-storey “cultural experience and exhibition” honouring the music history and legacy of the Fab Four.
Approval was granted unanimously at a planning meeting on Tuesday night despite concerns raised by the street’s tailoring businesses over the impact of tourism.

blocks.caption: 3 Savile Row in central London. Photograph: stockeurope/Alamy

blocks.text: The attraction will be subject to a number of conditions, including a restriction on live music on the rooftop. The use of amplified music will be permitted, but it will have to be at a controlled noise level. A noise report assessing the terrace was submitted, which the council’s environmental service deemed acceptable subject to such conditions.

Apple Corps, the intellectual property company established by the Beatles in 1968, re-acquired the building – which was the band’s headquarters between 1968 and 1972 – in May, announcing plans to open it to the public in 2027. Speaking at the meeting, the councillor Iman Less described it as the “coolest application I’ve ever done”.

The venue will include a basement cafe-bar, where the band partially recorded the album Let It Be, a replica of a studio they worked in and an exhibition shop. Apple Corps said it could attract as many as 900 visitors a day during the week and 1,140 a day at weekends.

blocks.caption: The Beatles performing on the rooftop of 3 Savile Row. Photograph: Hoberman Publishing/Alamy

blocks.text: A number of objections relating to general noise, disturbance and visitor numbers were received as part of the application. The Savile Row Bespoke Association, an organisation representing the area’s tailors, said the street’s narrow pavements “would lead to dangerous congestion and have a significant negative impact on those who visit and work” there.
But the planning committeewas told that the attraction would operate a live booking system rather than allowing walk-ins to prevent queues forming outside.

John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr – along with the US musician Billy Preston on electric piano – took to the roof on 30 January 1969 for an unannounced performance that became the Beatles’ final live appearance in public.

blocks.caption: The blue plaque commemorating the Beatles last live performance. Photograph: Mark Phillips/Alamy

blocks.text: The chief executive of Apple Corps, Tom Greene, revealed that McCartney had sent a letter to the committee expressing “how much the building means to him personally”.
He said the address would feature in the forthcoming Beatles biopics, which Sam Mendes is directing and which are scheduled for release as a quartet of films in 2028.

The deputy leader of Westminster council, Tim Barnes, said: “3 Savile Row has an extraordinary place in British music history. This is where the Beatles worked, recorded, and ultimately played their final public performance on a rooftop above the streets of Mayfair.

“We’re incredibly proud of Westminster’s cultural heritage and we want to see historic places like this continue to play a part in the life of our city. These plans will give fans from around the world the opportunity to get back to where a remarkable piece of music history actually happened.”
